attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, written in his own voice. He is not quoting anyone else.

semantics.note: An unhedged statement about current corporate use: 'mostly', 'limited ways' and reliability concern are all kept. It is correctly classed as an observation of the present state, not a forecast.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary and fair: most large customers use LLMs in limited ways, partly because of reliability concerns. Setting the window to early 2025 up to the post date is reasonable for a present-tense claim. The result here turns on missing evidence, not on how the claim is read.

evidence.note: Board survey with fieldwork Jan–Feb 2025: selective pilots 41%, scaling 25%, output inaccuracy named as a risk by 45%. Company sizes are mixed, the sample is directors, and there is no breakdown tying limited use to reliability among large companies. It leans toward caution but cannot settle the majority claim.

Survey of large North American organisations showing deployment concentrated in testing and development. Fieldwork was December 2024 (before the target period), and it lumps security and output risk together. Context only.
Only establishes that the e2 survey was fielded in December 2024, so it falls outside the target period.

KPMG survey of companies with $1B+ revenue showing daily use of productivity tools rising. Fieldwork dates are not given and it says nothing about reliability-driven restriction. Frequent use does not show broad deployment, so it neither contradicts nor supports the claim.

reviews.rationale: No item gives representative data for Jan 1–Mar 27, 2025 on large corporate LLM customers that measures both limited deployment and reliability-driven caution. e1 is in the window but mixes company sizes and reports its measures separately. e2/e3 cover December 2024. e4 has no fieldwork dates and no reliability link. The evidence leans toward caution but does not settle the claim.
